## Basics of AI

A fast, bullet-point primer on what AI is, where generative AI fits into the research workflow, and how to use it responsibly — condensed from Aalto's institutional guidance on AI in research.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this section you will be able to:

- Distinguish AI as a topic, a method, and a tool in research
- Identify where generative AI can help across the research lifecycle
- Recognize the misconduct risks of fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism
- Judge how much you can safely delegate to AI, based on your expertise and the stakes of the output
- Know when AI use must be disclosed — and how to write that disclosure
:::

### What Is AI?

Three roles AI can play in your research:

- **AI as a Topic** — studying AI itself (e.g. its ethics, impact, mechanisms)
- **AI as a Method** — using ML/AI as your analysis approach
- **AI as a Tool** — using AI applications to assist non-AI tasks

This section focuses on the third: **generative AI as a tool**.

### Generative AI Across the Research Lifecycle

Generative AI can assist at every stage:

- **Planning** — literature search, grant drafting, brainstorming
- **Data collection** — survey design, synthetic data, simulations
- **Pre-processing** — formatting, quality checks, cleaning
- **Analysis** — code generation, annotation
- **Preservation** — documentation, metadata
- **Sharing** — manuscript drafting, press releases
- **Reuse** — code documentation, dataset descriptions

### Avoiding Research Misconduct

Three risks to watch for:

- **Fabrication** — AI generates plausible but nonexistent text, references, or statistics
- **Falsification** — AI predicts a statistically likely output without genuine reasoning
- **Plagiarism** — AI synthesizes text without proper attribution

> If you cannot verify GenAI output, don't use it beyond brainstorming.

### Evaluating Risk: Expertise × Output-Risk

Weigh two factors before delegating a task to AI: your **expertise** on it, and the **importance of the output** (e.g. peer-reviewed claim vs. low-stakes draft).

- **High expertise, high risk** — OK to use AI, but only for simple sub-tasks you can fully review
- **Low expertise, high risk** — use AI only for brainstorming; go back to original sources
- **High expertise, low risk** — safe to delegate most of the work to AI
- **Low expertise, low risk** — usable, but accept a non-zero chance of error

### Disclosing AI Use

- **No declaration needed** — grammar and typo fixes only
- **Declaration required** — text synthesis, code generation, figure creation, analysis suggestions, section drafting
- **AI-generated images** — acceptable only to illustrate methodology; never to illustrate results
- **Disclosure template**:

  > During preparation, author(s) used [TOOL] for [REASON]. Content was reviewed; author(s) take full responsibility.

::: {.callout-note}
## Takeaways

- AI in research is a tool, a method, or a topic — know which role it's playing
- Generative AI can help at every stage of the research lifecycle, not just writing
- Never publish AI output you have not personally verified
- Match how much you delegate to your own expertise and the stakes of the output
- Disclose substantive AI use — grammar fixes are the only exception
:::

## References

1. Aalto University. (n.d.). *Best Practices for AI Use in Research Work*. [aalto.fi](https://www.aalto.fi/en/research-art/best-practices-for-ai-use-in-research-work)

## Basics of Large Language Models and AI Agents

Large language models (LLMs) are the engine behind today's AI tools; agents are what let them take action. This section builds intuition for both, using simple word- and letter-prediction examples.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this section you will be able to:

- Explain, at an intuitive level, how an LLM predicts its next word
- Describe how "temperature" controls the randomness of generated text
- Read a letter-pair probability heatmap as a simple example of statistical prediction
- Distinguish the model (word generator) from the harness (what lets it take actions)
- Describe the agent loop: think → call a tool → observe → repeat
- Use the core vocabulary of AI agents: model, scaffolding, harness, sub-agent

:::

### What Does a Large Language Model Actually Do?

- An LLM is, at its core, a **next-word prediction machine**: given the text so far, it predicts the most likely word to come next — then repeats, one word at a time
- A simple version of the same idea: guessing the next **letter**. If a word starts with "q", almost everyone guesses "u" next — not a rule anyone taught you, but a statistical pattern absorbed from years of reading English

![Probability of each pair of letters in typical English text — first letter across the top, second letter down the side; darker/more saturated cells are more probable pairs. Note how empty the "q" column is except at "u". (Source: Stephen Wolfram, "What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?", 2023)](images/ch01/letter-pair-heatmap.png){fig-alt="26x26 heatmap grid of English letter-pair probabilities, rows and columns labeled a to z, with the q column almost empty except at row u"}

- LLMs do the same thing as this heatmap, just at the scale of whole words (technically "tokens") instead of letters, learned from vast amounts of text rather than a 26×26 grid

### Temperature: How Predictable Should the Output Be?

- **Temperature 0** — always pick the single most likely next word: deterministic, but quickly repetitive. Prompted with "The best thing about AI is its ability to…":

  > The best thing about AI is its ability to learn from experience. It's not just a matter of learning from experience, it's learning from the world around you. The AI is a very good example of this. It's a very good example of how to use AI to improve your life. It's a very good example of how to use AI to improve your life. […]

- **Temperature 0.8** — sometimes pick a "non-top" word at random instead: more varied text. Building up the same prompt word by word:

  > The best thing about AI is its ability to,
  > The best thing about AI is its ability to create,
  > The best thing about AI is its ability to create worlds,
  > The best thing about AI is its ability to create worlds that,
  > The best thing about AI is its ability to create worlds that are,
  > The best thing about AI is its ability to create worlds that are both,
  > The best thing about AI is its ability to create worlds that are both exciting,

- Because the choice is random, repeating the same prompt at temperature 0.8 gives a different answer every time:
  - "…its ability to learn. I've always liked the"
  - "…its ability to really come into your world and just"
  - "…its ability to examine human behavior and the way it"
  - "…its ability to do a great job of teaching us"
  - "…its ability to create real tasks, but you can"
- **Trade-off**: low temperature = safe but dull and repetitive; high temperature = varied and more "creative," at the cost of predictability and coherence

### From Word Generators to Agents

- An **AI agent** = a language model (the "brain," generating words) + a **harness** (the "body," letting it take actions)
- The model reasons about what to do and, when it needs to act, outputs a **tool call**: structured text that says "run this"
- The harness executes that tool call (e.g. run code, send an email, search the web) and feeds the result back into the model's context
- The loop repeats — think, act, observe — until the task is done
- The harness also manages the model's limited working memory (its **context window**): chat history, files, and tool outputs all go in, and once it fills up, the harness compresses it
- The harness can delegate parts of a task to other agent instances (**sub-agents**), sometimes in parallel

![An agent is a model (the "intelligence box") plus a harness (manages execution) plus scaffolding (defines behavior); a harness can spin up sub-agents. (Source: Hugging Face, "The AI Agents Glossary", 2025)](images/ch01/agent-diagram.png){fig-alt="Diagram showing an Agent box containing Harness, Scaffold, and Model boxes, with an arrow down to a Sub-Agent box"}

- For the more precise vocabulary around agents — model vs. scaffolding vs. harness vs. sub-agent — see the Hugging Face agent glossary in the references below

::: {.callout-note}
## Takeaways

- An LLM is fundamentally a next-word predictor, trained on statistical patterns in huge amounts of text
- Temperature controls the trade-off between predictable-but-repetitive and varied-but-less-coherent output
- An agent is a model plus a harness: the model decides what to do, the harness lets it actually do it
- The think → act → observe loop, plus context-window management, is what turns a word generator into something that can complete multi-step tasks
:::
